analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers swap costly private student loans for lower-rate federal loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee that was referred it; it died in 2011 with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let people who borrowed private student loans to pay for college trade those loans in for federal ones. The new loans would carry the lower, fixed interest rates of federal Stafford or PLUS loans, plus federal repayment protections like income-based and forgiveness options. To qualify, borrowers had to be current on their private loan, not in default, and have been eligible for the federal loan they didn't originally take. The program would have been temporary, covering loans taken between 1994 and 2010.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers stuck with high-interest private student loans — often taken out before they understood federal options — would pay less interest and gain federal repayment protections such as flexible repayment plans and loan forgiveness programs. The bill also directed a national campaign to tell borrowers about these benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private student loan borrowers paying high rates

how_it_helps.text: Eligible borrowers could refinance private education loans at the interest rate of unsubsidized Stafford loans or federal Direct PLUS loans, replacing variable, credit-priced private rates with fixed federal rates [S2][S3].
Refinanced loans would carry the same repayment terms, conditions, and benefits as federal Direct Consolidation Loans, including federal repayment protections private lenders do not offer [S2][S3].

The Secretary of Education would run a national awareness campaign explaining the advantages of federal student loans over private loans, including repayment options, forgiveness opportunities, and fixed rates [S2][S3].
Loan proceeds would be paid directly to the private lender to discharge the old debt, so the swap would actually retire the high-cost loan rather than add new money to the borrower [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders would lose the high-interest loans they hold when borrowers refinance into cheaper federal loans, and the federal government would take on the new loans and administer the program, funded by 'such sums as may be necessary' [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student lenders and the federal loan program

drawbacks.text: The program is temporary and narrow: it covers only private loans taken between July 1, 1994 and July 1, 2010, caps the refinanced amount at federal Stafford borrowing limits for undergraduates and graduates, and excludes borrowers in default or more than 90 days delinquent — so the borrowers in the worst trouble get no help [S3].
PLUS-loan refinancing requires a clean credit history and borrowers must have made at least two consecutive payments, leaving out people who fell behind early [S2][S3].

The bill leaves funding open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary'), so taxpayers would bear whatever the swap costs, and the federal direct loan program would carry the refinanced debt instead of private investors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers holding expensive private loans, the deal is straightforwardly good: a lower fixed rate and federal protections in exchange for moving the debt to the federal books. The honest costs are that it does nothing for borrowers already in default, the refinance caps leave some balances on private terms, and the open-ended federal cost was never scored. As drafted it was a targeted rescue, not a blanket bailout.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was introduced and immediately sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on July 30, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S1][S5].
The committee never reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled in the Senate or House, and the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 with the bill still in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders keep their existing high-interest loan portfolios unchallenged, and no borrower gets the federal refinancing option.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Private Student Loan Debt Swap Act and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; it received no hearing action, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Private student loan industry
against.role: Lenders and servicers holding private education loans
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial interest in blocking refinancing that would pay off their loans with cheaper federal debt; the record shows no floor fight because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no measurable support or opposition by party [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders and servicers
industries.note: The bill would let borrowers pay off private loans with cheaper fixed-rate federal loans, stripping lenders of high-interest receivables and future interest income. Borrowers' savings are exactly the lenders' lost revenue.

The bill would route the refinanced debt through federal direct loans, making the federal program the permanent channel for this group of borrowers and taking on their debt at public cost. Borrowers gain federal protections in the process.
